claims.text: The as-cast HfNbTiVAl10 alloy has a hierarchical heterostructure containing nanoscale interfaces, phase boundaries, and lamellar features.
A physics-informed machine-learning model can fuse high-resolution microscopy descriptors with experimental tensile and fracture data.
The proposed model will predict Young’s modulus of HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed model will predict the yield strength of HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed model will predict fracture initiation and propagation behavior of HfNbTiVAl10.
The model will incorporate strain rate and temperature as boundary conditions.
Image analysis can quantify nanoscale interfaces, phase boundaries, and lamellar features for use as model descriptors.
Embedding physics constraints and detailed microstructural signatures will connect hierarchical structural features to macroscopic mechanical responses.
Fusing physics constraints with microstructural descriptors will capture coupled elastic and fracture behavior.
The proposed approach will reduce reliance on computationally expensive conventional simulations.
The proposed model will make predictions at least 10 times faster than traditional simulations.
The proposed model will reduce prediction errors by approximately 10–20% relative to existing simulation-based approaches.
Established finite-element and atomistic multiscale methods are currently used for HfNbTiVAl10 predictions.
The approach may fail when imaging resolution is insufficient to resolve critical nanoscale features.
The approach may fail at very high strain rates or temperatures where dynamic effects dominate.
The approach may fail when training data do not represent the variability of the hierarchical microstructure.
Independent tests will measure Young’s modulus, 0.2% offset yield strength, fracture initiation and propagation metrics, and prediction time.
The hypothesis is falsified if prediction deviations exceed approximately 20% or speedup is less than a factor of 10 relative to conventional simulations.

contradictions.description: The stated testing conditions restrict evaluation to room temperature, whereas the falsification design calls for comparison across multiple temperatures.
